---
title: "Finding sentence boundaries"
subtitle: "Compare three ways to split text into sentences"
description: "Learn why sentence segmentation can fail on abbreviations, decimals, initials, titles, and headings."
categories: [sentences and paragraphs, sentence segmentation, workforce research]
---

The coordinator counts sentences on a constructed page with flyer, pay, and
job-board text. The lesson then compares sentence boundaries in the separate
28-row Riverton file.

The page contains `Dr.`, `a.m.`, `$18.50`, and a heading without a period.
Those forms complicate sentence counts. A **sentence boundary** marks where
one sentence ends and the next begins. The team must state its boundary rule
before interpreting the count.

::: {.callout-note}
The Riverton page and CSV rows are fictional teaching data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain why sentence segmentation is harder than splitting on periods.
- compare an author-marked sentence count with three splitters.
- examine the fragments each splitter creates.
- use spaCy sentence identifiers from `spacy_parse()`.
- explain why the Riverton CSV already contains an upstream boundary choice.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Build a passage with difficult boundaries

readr reads the Riverton CSV, while dplyr and tibble build tables. purrr and
stringr execute the small splitters. tokenizers supplies a package splitter, and
spacyr calls a trained parser. A **splitter** is a rule or model that marks
text boundaries.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tokenizers)
library(spacyr)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

passage <- str_c(
  "RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE\n",
  "Dr. Vale said shifts start at 6 a.m.\n",
  "Pay is $18.50 per hour.\n",
  "J. Rivera can apply by Friday\n",
  "Bring a photo ID."
)

expected_sentences <- c(
  "RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE",
  "Dr. Vale said shifts start at 6 a.m.",
  "Pay is $18.50 per hour.",
  "J. Rivera can apply by Friday",
  "Bring a photo ID."
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    expected_number = seq_along(expected_sentences),
    sentence = expected_sentences
  ),
  col.names = c("Expected sentence", "Author-marked text"),
  caption = "The five expected sentence boundaries",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(c(
  "readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "purrr", "stringr", "tokenizers", "spacyr"
) %in% loadedNamespaces()))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(length(expected_sentences), 5L),
  any(str_detect(sentences$text, fixed("Apply by October 15")))
)
```

The expected-answer list has five sentences. Because that list and the examples
share an author, agreement with it is a lesson check rather than an accuracy
estimate. The first sentence is a flyer-style heading with no punctuation. The
next three contain a title, an abbreviation, a decimal, and an initial.

## Compare three splitters

The naive rule below splits text at every full stop. `tokenizers` uses a
sentence-splitting rule from an R package. spaCy uses a trained English pipeline.
`spacy_parse()` returns one row per token, and its `sentence_id` column records
the boundary spaCy chose.

```{r}
split_on_full_stop <- function(text) {
  text |>
    str_split(fixed(".")) |>
    pluck(1) |>
    str_trim() |>
    discard(\(piece) identical(piece, ""))
}

join_spacy_tokens <- function(tokens) {
  str_c(tokens, collapse = " ") |>
    str_squish() |>
    str_replace_all(fixed(" ."), ".") |>
    str_replace_all(fixed(" ,"), ",") |>
    str_replace_all(fixed("$ "), "$")
}

naive_pieces <- split_on_full_stop(passage)
tokenizer_pieces <- tokenize_sentences(passage)[[1]]

source("R/use-spacy.R")
pipeline <- use_project_spacy()
spacy_metadata <- spacy_pipeline_version()
spacy_tokens <- spacy_parse(
  setNames(passage, "test_passage"),
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE
)
spacy_finalize()

spacy_pieces <- spacy_tokens |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(piece = join_spacy_tokens(token), .by = sentence_id) |>
  pull(piece)

split_results <- bind_rows(
  tibble(splitter = "split on full stops", piece = naive_pieces),
  tibble(splitter = "tokenizers::tokenize_sentences()", piece = tokenizer_pieces),
  tibble(splitter = "spaCy sentence_id", piece = spacy_pieces)
) |>
  mutate(
    splitter = factor(
      splitter,
      levels = c(
        "split on full stops",
        "tokenizers::tokenize_sentences()",
        "spaCy sentence_id"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(splitter) |>
  group_by(splitter) |>
  mutate(
    piece_number = row_number(),
    exact_expected_sentence = piece %in% expected_sentences
  ) |>
  ungroup()

splitter_scores <- split_results |>
  summarise(
    pieces_found = n(),
    exact_expected_pieces = sum(exact_expected_sentence),
    .by = splitter
  ) |>
  mutate(
    expected_pieces = length(expected_sentences),
    count_difference = pieces_found - expected_pieces,
    matches_expected_count = pieces_found == expected_pieces
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| html-table-processing: none

knitr::kable(
  splitter_scores,
  col.names = c(
    "Splitter",
    "Pieces found",
    "Exact pieces",
    "Expected pieces",
    "Difference",
    "Count matches"
  ),
  caption = "Splitter counts compared with the five expected sentences",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  split_results |>
    mutate(exact_expected_sentence = if_else(exact_expected_sentence, "yes", "no")),
  col.names = c("Splitter", "Piece", "Piece number", "Exact expected sentence"),
  caption = "Where each splitter puts the boundaries",
  format = "html",
  table.attr = 'class="caption-top table table-sm table-striped small" style="white-space: pre-line;"',
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(spacy_metadata$version, "3.8.0"),
  identical(spacy_metadata$license, "MIT"),
  identical(spacy_metadata$spacy, "3.8.7"),
  identical(length(naive_pieces), 7L),
  identical(length(tokenizer_pieces), 5L),
  identical(length(spacy_pieces), 2L),
  identical(splitter_scores$pieces_found, c(7L, 5L, 2L)),
  identical(splitter_scores$exact_expected_pieces, c(0L, 1L, 0L)),
  identical(splitter_scores$count_difference, c(2L, 0L, -3L))
)
```

The naive rule finds seven pieces and none is one of the five expected
sentences. It splits `Dr.`, `a.m.`, `$18.50`, and `J.`. The package splitter
returns the expected count, but only one piece exactly matches an expected sentence. It
attaches `Dr.` to the heading and separates `J.` from the name.

spaCy returns two pieces. It preserves `Dr. Vale` and `a.m.` but combines
lines into fewer sentences than the layout implies. The pipeline uses syntax
instead of the line-break boundaries that the flyer requires.

The code reconstructs spaCy pieces from tokens and does not preserve the
original spaces or line breaks. The exact-match column therefore compares
reconstructed text rather than the copied page. Equal piece counts alone do
not establish correct segmentation. A splitter can return the expected number
of pieces with incorrect boundary positions.

## Examine the Riverton rows

The file creator assigned one sentence or flyer line to each of the 28
Riverton rows. This **upstream boundary choice** occurs before the lesson reads
the file.

```{r}
sentence_piece_counts <- tokenize_sentences(sentences$text) |>
  map_int(length)

row_boundary_summary <- sentences |>
  mutate(sentence_pieces = sentence_piece_counts) |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    tokenizer_pieces = sum(sentence_pieces),
    .by = document_id
  )

flyer_rows <- sentences |>
  filter(document_id == "F001") |>
  nrow()

job_rows <- sentences |>
  filter(document_id != "F001") |>
  nrow()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  row_boundary_summary,
  col.names = c("Document ID", "Rows", "Sentence pieces"),
  caption = "Sentence splitting agrees with the stored Riverton rows",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(sentence_piece_counts, rep(1L, 28L)),
  identical(sum(row_boundary_summary$rows), 28L),
  identical(sum(row_boundary_summary$tokenizer_pieces), 28L),
  identical(flyer_rows, 6L),
  identical(job_rows, 22L)
)
```

For these stored rows, the package splitter returns one sentence piece for every
row. That agreement does not prove the rows are the only possible boundaries. It
only shows agreement between this file and this splitter on the teaching set.

## What to remember

- Sentence segmentation marks where one sentence ends and another begins.
- A full stop can appear inside titles, initials, abbreviations, and decimals.
- In the test passage, the three splitters return 7, 5, and 2 pieces.
- A correct count can still hide wrong boundaries.
- Rebuilding model output from tokens can change the text that the code scores.
- The 28 Riverton rows already contain one upstream boundary choice.

For the copied page, five expected sentences are a human layout choice. For the
CSV, 28 one-row sentence units are an upstream data choice. Both counts depend on
the rule named beside them.
